title: The Winter List
subtitle: Ninebark, Montana Territory, November to Christmas 1864

listing.title: The Winter List ❄️
listing.blurb: Montana Territory, winter 1864. Road agents are robbing the gold coaches out of Ninebark, a messenger is dead, and a secret vigilance committee has started hanging men by lantern light. Nobody knows who sits on it. Nobody knows whose name is next on its list, and somebody has written in one name that nobody in camp could have known. Stand between the road agents and the rope, and bring the truth to a court before the snow shuts the road. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Ninebark is a gold camp of two thousand people strung for four miles along a gulch in the mountains of the new Montana Territory, a long day's coach ride north of Bannack. It is six months old, rich, cold, and frightened. Since October, road agents have robbed the Thursday treasure coach on the Rattlesnake Grade three times, and on 3 November they shot the express messenger, Will Danforth, dead on the box. The next day the camp's leading merchants met in the back of Obadiah Wexford's store and swore themselves into a secret vigilance committee, forty men known to one another by number, as the committees of Alder Gulch and Bannack had done the winter before. That afternoon they caught a horse-holder named Jack Tillery with Danforth's watch in his pocket. Under the rope on 6 November, promised his life, Tillery named ten names; the committee wrote them down and hanged him anyway. On 10 November it hanged the second name, an Irish miner called Patrick Kehoe. The list now has twelve names on it, in two columns, HANG and BANISH, and nobody outside the committee knows whose they are. The party arrives on the up coach on Monday 14 November. Over six weeks they ride guard on a robbed coach, find out what is on the list and how it was made, stand in a lantern-lit warehouse while the committee holds a trial with a verdict already written, and face the reckoning on the last coach of the season, the Thursday before Christmas, with a blizzard coming and the road about to close for the winter. The road agents are real and they are murderers. The committee is real, and so are its murders. Between them stands one schoolmaster sheriff with a tin star, a federal deputy whose name is already on the list, and whatever the party decides to be. The truth, which the GM holds in controlFile, is that the list was not Tillery's: the road agents' chief, a well-liked station keeper who sits on the committee, gave Tillery the names, and is using the committee to hang every man who could identify his gang. The twelfth name on the list belongs to a man nobody in Ninebark had ever heard of. Only someone who had opened the mail could have known it.
hook: Monday 14 November 1864, a little after noon, the up coach from Bannack. You have been on it since dawn: nine passengers inside, two on the roof, the driver and a Californio messenger with a coach gun on the box, and the mail. The coach stopped at Fiddler's Station at the top of the Rattlesnake Grade to change horses, and the station keeper, a big, cheerful man named Warrick Sefton, gave you hot coffee and venison stew and would not take your money: 'not on a cold day, not from friends of the Beaverhead Express.' Now the road comes down out of the timber into Ninebark Gulch, and the camp opens below you: a mile of log stores and false fronts, smoke from a thousand chimneys, sluice boxes frozen white along the creek, and the noise of a town that never stops working. Where the road comes into the gulch, beside it, there is a slaughter corral with a high log gateway. Someone has nailed a board across the top of the gate. Painted on the board, in black, in neat capitals, is a single word: WARNED. The messenger on the box looks at it, and then at the road ahead, and does not say anything at all. In front of Wexford's store a crowd is reading a printed notice on the door. A thin, grey, bespectacled man with a tin star is standing in front of it with his arms folded, as if he could stop people reading it by standing there. The notice says: TO THE PEOPLE OF NINEBARK. THE NAMES ARE KNOWN. LET THE GUILTY LEAVE THIS CAMP WHILE THEY STILL CAN. BY ORDER, THE COMMITTEE OF VIGILANCE.

setting.name: Ninebark Gulch and the Bannack road, Montana Territory, 14 November to 24 December 1864
setting.description: Ninebark, Ninebark Gulch, Fiddler's Station, the Rattlesnake Grade, Deadfall Canyon and every person in this campaign are fictional; Montana Territory, Bannack, Alder Gulch, Salt Lake City, the Civil War and the history around them are real. Congress created Montana Territory on 26 May 1864, carving it out of Idaho; its capital is Bannack, its first legislature will meet there on Monday 12 December 1864, and until then most of its law is a governor, a handful of appointed judges and marshals, and the by-laws of each mining district, enforced by miners' courts and elected district sheriffs. The winter before, from December 1863 to February 1864, vigilance committees at Alder Gulch and Bannack hanged more than twenty men without trial, and many respectable people said it had been necessary. The campaign does not say so. Ninebark was struck in May 1864: placer gold in the gravels of Ninebark Creek and the benches above it, ten claims to the mile, and a town of two thousand miners, merchants, packers, gamblers, laundresses, saloon keepers and families that grew up in a summer. Everything it eats, drinks and wears comes over the mountains by mule train or wagon from Salt Lake City, three hundred and fifty miles south; when the snow closes the passes, prices double. Its gold goes out the same way, on the Beaverhead Express Company's Thursday coach to Bannack and on to Salt Lake City, carrying the miners' dust in iron-bound treasure boxes. Money is gold dust, weighed on a scale in every store and saloon at eighteen dollars the ounce, and paper greenbacks, which buy about forty cents on the dollar in gold this winter. The Civil War is still being fought. Ninebark's people are Union men and Missouri secessionists, many of whom came west to get away from the war or the draft; Irish and German miners; Californio and Sonoran packers, who carry most of the freight; Cornish hard-rock men, a few; free Black men and women from Illinois, Missouri and Colorado; Canadian voyageurs' sons; New Englanders with law books; and women who keep boarding houses, deal faro, wash, nurse and stake claims. Lincoln's re-election on 8 November will reach the camp by coach from the Salt Lake City telegraph late in the month, and the camp will not take it quietly.
setting.atmosphere: Snow and smoke. The gulch is narrow and steep and the sun is off it by three in the afternoon; the cold comes down from the peaks at night and the creek freezes at the edges, then in the middle. Woodsmoke hangs in the gulch all day. The sounds are the sounds of work that does not stop for the season: picks on frozen gravel, rockers and sluices running where there is still water, the blacksmith's hammer, a hurdy-gurdy fiddle at the Union Saloon, the coach horn on the Bannack road, mules braying in the packers' corrals. The camp is loud by day and silent by night, because at night nobody is sure who is walking in the street. Lanterns move along the gulch after midnight, and people do not go to their windows. The committee's men wear flour-sack masks with eyeholes, or no masks at all and nobody admits to recognising them. The tone is a western paperback with the horror kept honest: hard winter, hard money, good horses, a gunfight on a grade that lasts eight seconds, and a hanging that the camp will spend twenty years pretending was necessary. The hangings are crimes and they are horrible. The GM never presents one as justice, as satisfying, or as a solution: they are frightening, ugly, quick and wrong, and the people who watch them know it and look away. The committee's men are not monsters: most of them are frightened merchants and miners who want the robberies to stop, and that is what makes them dangerous. The road agents are not romantic either: they are thieves who shot a man reaching for his spectacles.

regions.name: Ninebark
regions.description: The camp: one long crooked street, Water Street, running down the gulch beside the creek for a mile, with cross streets climbing the hillsides. Obadiah Wexford's store, the biggest building in camp, two storeys of sawn lumber with a warehouse behind it, where the committee was founded and meets. The Beaverhead Express Company's office, where Simeon Prothero weighs and seals the dust and keeps the treasure boxes in a brick vault. Mordecai Pottinger's Union Saloon, with a flag over the door, a hurdy-gurdy house upstairs and Leonie Fairbairn's faro bank in the corner. Horatio Grimsby's law office, with a safe. The district sheriff's office and jail, a log cabin with one barred window. Gabriel Tennant's forge. Moira Kehoe's boarding house. The Ninebark Sentinel, a weekly printed on a hand press by Jonas Fenley. Two churches, a Catholic priest who comes once a month, three hotels, eleven saloons, a bathhouse, an assay office and a dentist. At the foot of the gulch, where the Bannack road comes in, the slaughter corral with its log gateway, where the committee hangs men.

regions.name: The Diggings and the Upper Bench
regions.description: Above and below the town, Ninebark Creek is claims from wall to wall: shafts, windlasses, sluices, rockers, ditches, cabins and tents, numbered from Discovery up and down the creek. The Number Three claim, where Patrick Kehoe worked the night shift, is a deep shaft below town with a windlass house and a stove. August Ruhl's claims, worked by hired hands including two Scandinavians, are above town. The Upper Bench, a gravel terrace three hundred feet above the creek, is newer ground, where Ada Brockway has her claim. In winter the creek claims are worked by drifting under the frozen gravel by candlelight, and the night shift sees everything that moves on the road.

regions.name: The Bannack Road: Fiddler's Station and the Rattlesnake Grade
regions.description: The coach road leaves Ninebark to the south, climbs eleven miles through timber to a pass, and at the top of the pass reaches Fiddler's Station: the Beaverhead Express Company's swing station, where the coach changes horses, the passengers eat, and the treasure boxes are carried off the coach and back on while the teams are changed. The station keeper, Warrick Sefton, has a log house, a barn with a hayloft, corrals, a smithy shed and a washing line. Below the station the road drops three miles down the Rattlesnake Grade, a narrow shelf with a cliff on one side and timber on the other, a hairpin called the Elbow, and a creek ford at the bottom. All three robberies happened between the Elbow and the ford. From the ridge above the grade, a man with field glasses can see Fiddler's Station's yard.

regions.name: Deadfall Canyon and the High Country
regions.description: West of the road the mountains break into side canyons choked with timber and old blowdown. Deadfall Canyon is the wildest, a hidden valley two hours' ride from Fiddler's Station by a trail nobody uses, with a spring, a meadow of winter grass and a trapper's cabin. The packers wintered mules there in 1863. The road agents winter there now. In December, snow closes the high country for weeks at a time, and the only safe way into the canyon is the way the gang uses, past the station; Chelo Arvizu knows another, from the top.

campaignRules.name: The Winter Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs from Monday 14 November to Saturday 24 December 1864, and every faction acts on the calendar whether or not the players are watching. vg-scenario-001 is the robbed coach (14 to 19 November); vg-scenario-002 the list (20 November to 3 December); vg-scenario-003 the trial that isn't (4 to 10 December); vg-scenario-004 the reckoning (11 to 24 December). Track the date openly. The treasure coach runs down to Bannack every Thursday and the up coach comes in on Mondays and Saturdays, weather permitting. If the players do not interfere, this happens. THE ROAD AGENTS: Thursday 17 November, they rob the down coach on the Rattlesnake Grade (vg-scenario-001); they lie low through the storm; on Thursday 22 December they rob the last coach of the season, carrying $112,000, burn Fiddler's Station so that its keeper appears to have died in the fire, and go over the pass to Idaho with the cache. THE COMMITTEE: Friday 18 November, a warning card under Leonie Fairbairn's door; Tuesday 22 November at midnight they seize Tobiah Corder, a Missouri teamster on the list, and hang him at dawn on Wednesday 23 November; Thursday 24 November, Thanksgiving, the committee's men march in the street; Friday 25 November, the news of Lincoln's re-election arrives and the Union Saloon and the Missourians fight; the storm closes the road from Tuesday 29 November to Friday 2 December; Tuesday 6 December at midnight they seize Sheriff Barnabas Wyndham and Torvald Fjeld, 'the Swede at Ruhl's', and try them in Wexford's warehouse with the verdict already written; Wednesday 7 December they banish Moira Kehoe and Leonie Fairbairn; on Thursday 22 December, the same night as the last coach, Mordecai Pottinger's men mean to hang every name left on the list. THE LAW: Thursday 8 December, a probate judge appointed for the district, Elihu Marten, arrives on the up coach with authority to hold an examining court; Monday 12 December, the first territorial legislature meets at Bannack. A party that does nothing sees at least seven more men hanged, two women driven into the snow, a federal deputy murdered, and the road agents gone over the pass with more than $200,000 in dust.

campaignRules.name: The List
campaignRules.description: The committee's list is one sheet of ruled foolscap in Horatio Grimsby's safe, written by Grimsby in ink at Jack Tillery's 'confession' on the morning of Sunday 6 November, with one name added by the Executive in ink on 11 November and one, the last, in pencil. The players should learn it a name at a time; the GM reveals the whole sheet only when the party gets hold of it or a copy (vg-scenario-002). HANG: 1. Judd Ferrier. 2. Wick Brill. 3. Patrick Kehoe (struck through: hanged 10 November). 4. Micah Garrick. 5. 'The sheriff who lets them go' (Barnabas Wyndham). 6. Tobiah Corder. 7. August Ruhl. 8. Fergal McGarvey of the Beaverhead Crossing. 9. 'The Swede at Ruhl's'. BANISH: 10. 'The faro woman at the Union' (Leonie Fairbairn). 11. 'The widow Kehoe, for harbouring' (added by the committee's Executive on 11 November, in ink). 12., in pencil, in a different hand, below a ruled line: 'C. Hartigan. Federel man. Comes on the coach. In it with them.' Two names are road agents (Ferrier, Brill: Tillery named them himself, out of spite). The rest are innocent of these robberies. Micah Garrick's name is true of a different crime in a different territory, and the GM should agree with his player how much of that is known. If a pregen is not being played, the name stands for an NPC of that name who is still in camp, or who left in October, as the GM chooses. Before putting any player character's name into the committee's hands as a target, ask that player. When the committee acts on a name, it sends a warning card first (twenty-four hours) to every BANISH name and to any HANG name it hopes will simply run, as Tobiah Corder's did; to the rest it sends nothing. Then it comes at midnight with lanterns and masks, twelve to twenty men, and the party has until dawn.

campaignRules.name: Hangings Are Murder
campaignRules.description: Every hanging in this campaign is a murder, and the GM narrates it as one: quick, cold, botched more often than not, watched by people who look away, and remembered. Never present a hanging as satisfying, deserved or a solution, including the hanging of a guilty man; when the party catches a road agent the lawful course is the jail, the examining court and the territorial court, and the campaign rewards it. The committee is forty men known to each other by number, not name, sworn in Wexford's warehouse; it meets with an Executive of five who decide the names. Members are ordinary: merchants, miners, a lawyer, a saloon keeper, a station keeper. Most of them believe they are saving the camp. They can be argued with, frightened, shamed, outvoted or out-waited, and the more of them the party talks to as people, the more of them stop coming out at night. Use Vigilante (adversaries.json) for committee men in groups of four to eight, and the Lynch Mob for a full turnout, with its Mob Mind: a DC 15 Persuasion or Intimidation check as an action strips 2d10 hit points as people slink away, naming members aloud adds 1d10, and unmasking or arresting the ringleader breaks it at once; a Lawman's Stand Your Ground or a Preacher's Stand Between can break it as well. Firing into the mob costs Reputation for every townsman killed. Each time the party prevents a hanging without killing anyone, the committee loses 2d6 members who do not come out again. Each time a committee man is killed, it gains 1d6 frightened recruits and the camp's Reputation for the party falls by 1. The committee is not the villain and the road agents are not the heroes: both are killing people, and the party's job is to stop both.

campaignRules.name: Reputation
campaignRules.description: The party has one Reputation score in Ninebark (frontier.json reputation), starting at 0, tracked openly by the GM. It means 'do decent people trust you', not 'does the committee like you'. +1: saving the coach, catching a road agent alive, speaking up for a prisoner in public, paying debts, nursing the sick, giving testimony in court. -1: joining the committee, wearing a mask, shooting a man who has not drawn, being seen with Sefton's men after the truth is out, bullying a witness. -2: taking part in a hanging, or standing by at one when you could have spoken. At +3 the miners' meeting will vote for whatever the party proposes and Simeon Prothero will put them on the payroll; at -3 a warning card appears under their door. Separately, the committee keeps a WATCH on the party: 0 to 3. It rises by 1 each time they visibly interfere; at 2 a member is set to follow them; at 3 a party member's name goes into the BANISH column, or, if they have killed a committee man, the HANG column. Tell the players when Reputation changes; do not tell them the WATCH, but let them see its effects.

campaignRules.name: Three Clues
campaignRules.description: The mystery follows the three-clue rule: every conclusion has at least three clues in different places; looking in the right place with a sensible skill finds a core clue without a roll; rolls buy detail, speed or leverage; a failed roll costs time or Reputation, never the case. The conclusions are lettered A to E in controlFile and in each scenario's cluesAvailable. A: Patrick Kehoe was innocent. B: Tillery's confession was coached. C: the twelfth name could only have come from the mail, and the mail lay overnight at Fiddler's Station. D: the road agents work out of Fiddler's Station. E: Warrick Sefton is committee number 23 and the road agents' chief. If the party is stuck, have a companion lay out what they know in character, by the stove at Moira Kehoe's. The best evidence is evidence that a court can hear: a sworn witness, a ledger, a letter, a cast shoe, the cache. Remind the players, through Barnabas Wyndham or Judge Marten, that a confession under a rope is worth nothing in court, which is the whole point.

campaignRules.name: The 1864 Armory
campaignRules.description: Money is dollars, kept two ways: gold dust, weighed at $18 the ounce in every store, and greenbacks, which buy only about forty cents on the dollar in gold this winter; prices are in dust unless a merchant is cheating. Flour is $24 a sack in November and rising; a meal is 75 cents in dust; a room with board is $10 a week; a miner earns $6 a day. As the road closes in December, prices double. THIS IS AN 1860s CAMPAIGN: weapons are cap-and-ball or early rimfire. Allowed: Navy revolvers (.36, loaded with paper cartridges and percussion caps), pocket revolvers (.32 rimfire), single-shot pocket pistols, Henry repeating rifles (.44 rimfire), Spencer carbines (.56), muzzle-loading shotguns, sabers, knives and black-powder charges. NOT YET INVENTED: the heavy .45 cartridge Army revolver (equipment.json's 'Army revolver', 1870s on), the buffalo rifle (1870s) and dynamite (patented 1867). Never give these out as loot or stock. A randomly generated character who arrives with an Army revolver should swap it for a Navy revolver, .36 rounds and a spare cylinder before play begins; tell the player why. The ruleset's Navy revolver reload (two rounds an action) stands in for capping and ramming; a spare loaded cylinder swaps in as an action, or as a bonus action with Fast Hands. Adversary stat blocks written for later decades (Outlaw, Hired Gun, Gang Leader, Gunfighter, Fast Gun) attack with an Army Revolver: here, read it as a Navy revolver, same attack bonus, 1d8 plus the same modifier. Do not use the Dynamiter.

campaignRules.name: Snow and the Road
campaignRules.description: Use frontier.json weather_and_water for cold. From 20 November, any night spent outdoors without a fire and robes is a DC 12 CON save against a level of exhaustion; from 10 December, DC 15. The road: Ninebark to Fiddler's Station is eleven miles, three hours by coach, two on a good horse; the station to the ford at the foot of the Rattlesnake Grade is three miles; Bannack is a long day beyond. Snow on the grade makes it difficult terrain for riders and a DC 13 Riding check at the Elbow for anything faster than a walk. The great storm of 29 November to 2 December closes the road and the high country: no coach, no travel above the Upper Bench without snowshoes (Survival DC 15 to stay on a trail). Deadfall Canyon can be reached in winter only past Fiddler's Station, or from the top by a way Chelo Arvizu knows (Survival DC 14 with her, impossible without). Horses: a riding horse in camp costs $120 in dust and a winter's hay costs as much again; a horse that dies in the snow is a real loss (frontier.json horses_and_mounts). Showdowns (frontier.json showdowns) happen in the street, where the whole camp can see, and the camp judges them.

wildernessStarts.label: Ninebark: the notice on Wexford's door, Monday noon
Fiddler's Station: coffee and stew on the up coach
The Rattlesnake Grade: the Elbow, Thursday morning

explorationRules: This is a camp sandbox with a road running out of it, and the map is a schematic: Ninebark in its gulch at the top, the diggings around it, the slaughter corral at the foot of the gulch where the road comes in, the road south over the pass to Fiddler's Station, down the Rattlesnake Grade, and on to the Beaverhead Crossing and Bannack; Deadfall Canyon in the high country to the west. The unit of time is the half-day, and the Winter Clock (campaignRules) is the engine: every faction keeps moving while the party is busy somewhere else. Most scenes are a conversation across a counter, a stove, a faro layout or a forge with someone who is frightened and wants something, and the party should talk to everyone: the committee's members are ordinary people who can be turned one at a time. Run each scenario as a set of named places, with the road agents and the committee acting on their schedules and on what they could know. Nobody is omniscient. Sefton knows what the committee's Executive decides, what passes through his station and what his gang tells him; Wexford knows what the Executive tells him and is beginning to doubt it; Grimsby keeps the list and believes it; Pottinger hates Missourians and owes Leonie Fairbairn money; Barnabas Wyndham knows the coaches and nothing about the committee. Fights are short, loud and consequential, and a fight with the committee is a fight with the camp. Between scenes, let the winter breathe: woodsmoke, a dog barking down the gulch, the coach horn, a fiddle through a saloon wall, the creek freezing, lanterns moving after midnight. The players should finish knowing what a vigilance committee was, and that stopping one took more courage than joining it.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Ninebark, the Ninebark district, Fiddler's Station, the Rattlesnake Grade, Deadfall Canyon, the Beaverhead Express Company, the Ninebark Committee of Vigilance and every person in the campaign are fictional. Montana Territory, Bannack, Alder Gulch, the 1863 to 1864 vigilance hangings there, the territory's creation in May 1864, the first legislature of December 1864, the gold dust economy, greenbacks, Lincoln's re-election and the Civil War are real history. This is an analogue of the vigilance committees of the mining frontier, not a retelling of any one, and no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: Warrick Sefton, 44, the cheerful, generous keeper of Fiddler's Station, is the chief of the road agents. He came to the territory from Kansas in 1863 with debts and a talent for being liked, took the Beaverhead Express Company's station contract in June 1864, and saw at once that his station was the one place on the road where a stranger could learn, without asking, which coach was heavy: at Fiddler's the treasure boxes are carried off the coach and back on while the teams are changed, and a man who lifts a box knows its weight. He recruited four men he had known in Kansas and Colorado: Judd Ferrier, 36, the killer; Wick Brill, 30; Hank Crewe, 40; and Nels Eklund, 25, a Norwegian who took a job on August Ruhl's claims as cover and brings news from camp; and two hangers-on, Davy Renner, 19, and Jack Tillery, 23, a horse-holder and lookout. On a heavy Thursday Sefton hangs washing on the line in his yard, two shirts and a red blanket, which the lookout on the ridge above the grade can see through field glasses; nobody washes outdoors in a Montana November, and nobody has noticed. The gang waits in the timber below the Elbow, robs the coach between the Elbow and the ford, and rides back up through the timber into Fiddler's barn by early afternoon, where the horses are rubbed down and the dust goes under the barn floor; it is carried to the gang's cabin in Deadfall Canyon later. Sefton has never ridden on a robbery. The gang has taken $71,000 from three coaches: 13 October, 20 October, and 3 November, when Ferrier shot the messenger Will Danforth because Danforth reached for the coach gun. At noon on Friday 4 November the merchants formed the committee, and at three that afternoon Jack Tillery, drunk, tried to sell Danforth's watch in the Union Saloon and was locked in Wexford's root cellar. That night the up coach from Bannack was snowbound at Fiddler's Station, and Sefton, who did not yet know about Tillery, opened the mail sack, as he always does when the mail lies over, and read a letter from the territorial marshal to Simeon Prothero announcing that a deputy U.S. marshal named C. Hartigan would arrive in mid-November to investigate the robberies. He resealed it with a second wafer. At dawn on Saturday Nels Eklund rode up from camp to tell him Tillery was taken. Sefton had a problem: Tillery would name him. He rode to town ahead of the coach and asked to join the committee; Obadiah Wexford, who has eaten at his table a hundred times, swore him in at noon as number 23. On the night of Saturday 5 November Sefton volunteered to stand guard on Tillery in Wexford's root cellar, and offered him a bargain: at the confession, do not name me, name these men instead, and I will see that you are let go. He gave Tillery a list of men who could hurt the gang: Patrick Kehoe, who had seen Ferrier and Brill leading blown horses into Fiddler's corral on the afternoon of 3 November and had said so in the Union Saloon; Barnabas Wyndham, the sheriff, who was asking who knew which coaches were heavy; Fergal McGarvey, keeper of the rival Beaverhead Crossing roadhouse, who wanted Sefton's station contract and had told Prothero that Fiddler's 'kept funny hours'; August Ruhl, who had sacked Eklund and might ask why; and men chosen to make the list look like road agents to the committee: Tobiah Corder, a loud Missouri secessionist; 'the faro woman at the Union', whom Pottinger owed money and would be glad to see gone; and 'the Swede at Ruhl's', left vague on purpose, so that when the committee came to Ruhl's it would take the wrong Scandinavian and not Nels Eklund. Tillery named Sefton's names on the morning of 6 November, and added three of his own: Judd Ferrier and Wick Brill, who had left him to be caught, and Micah Garrick, whom he had seen with road agents in Idaho in 1863. The committee wrote them down and hanged Tillery at noon. Sefton voted for it. On Wednesday 9 November, at the Executive's meeting, Sefton added a name in pencil, in his own round, cramped hand, misspelling one word: 'C. Hartigan. Federel man. Comes on the coach. In it with them.' He said that Tillery had told him so in the cellar. Tillery could not have known it: he was locked up at three in the afternoon of 4 November, and the letter reached Ninebark on the up coach the next afternoon, and only Simeon Prothero and Barnabas Wyndham had read it. Only a man who had opened the mail could have known that name. On 10 November the committee hanged Patrick Kehoe. Sefton warned Ferrier and Brill, who went up to Deadfall Canyon. His plan now: keep the committee hanging every man who threatens him, rob the coach of 17 November, lie low through the storm, and on Thursday 22 December rob the last coach of the season, carrying the camp's winter clean-up, $112,000; that night burn Fiddler's Station with a body in it, a harmless old drifter he has taken in out of 'charity' and will drug with laudanum, so that the camp believes Warrick Sefton died defending his station; and ride over the pass to Idaho with the cache. On the same night, at Sefton's urging, Pottinger's hardliners mean to hang every name left on the list, so that every eye in Ninebark is on the slaughter corral and not the road.
suspects: Warrick Sefton, 44, keeper of Fiddler's Station, committee number 23: the road agents' chief. Motive: more than $200,000 in dust, and his neck. He fed Tillery the names, added Hartigan's in pencil, and pushes the committee to hang every man who could identify his gang. Plan: rob the last coach on 22 December, fake his death in a fire, leave for Idaho. THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Judd Ferrier, 36, road agent: the killer of Will Danforth. Tall, pale, quiet, with a scar through his left eyebrow and a habit of whistling 'Aura Lea'. Wintering in Deadfall Canyon. Will not be taken alive if he can help it.

Mordecai Pottinger, 50, owner of the Union Saloon, committee Executive: the most dangerous man on the committee who is not a road agent. A Radical Union man who sees a secessionist plot behind every robbery and wants the Missourians driven out. He owes Leonie Fairbairn $1,100. He did not rob anyone and he believes in the list; he is the man most eager to hang.

Horatio Grimsby, 39, lawyer, committee Executive, keeper of the list: the committee's 'prosecutor', who wrote down Tillery's confession and believes a confession under the rope is the best evidence there is. He has convinced himself the committee is a court. He tore the true cause of death out of Konrad Kranzler's certificate for Patrick Kehoe.

Obadiah Wexford, 58, merchant, president of the committee: the man who founded it, in his own warehouse, because his customers' gold was being stolen and nobody else would act. He is beginning to doubt, since Kehoe, and is frightened of what he made. He can be turned, and when he is, the committee splits.

Simeon Prothero, 45, agent of the Beaverhead Express Company: the man who knows which coach is heavy, and the most obvious inside man. He is honest, sick with worry, and losing his job if one more coach is robbed. He is not a member of the committee; he refused, which the committee holds against him.
redHerrings: Simeon Prothero. He knows every coach's treasure, he refused to join the committee, and he has been seen talking privately with Sheriff Wyndham. Pottinger and Grimsby suspect him, and so will a party that starts with 'who knew?'. Barnabas's ledger shows the answer to 'who knew?' includes everyone at Fiddler's Station.

The Missourians. Pottinger's theory: the robberies are a secessionist ring sending gold to the Confederacy. Tobiah Corder is a loud Missouri man who drinks to Jefferson Davis in the Union Saloon to annoy Pottinger and owns a fast horse. He has nothing to do with the robberies; he was in the district jail for being drunk from the evening of 2 November to noon on the 3rd, by Barnabas's own book.

Fergal McGarvey of the Beaverhead Crossing, the rival roadhouse below the ford. His roadhouse is the nearest building to the robbery site, his hostler has a new coat, and he hates Sefton. He wants the station contract and told Prothero that Fiddler's kept funny hours, which is true; his hostler won the coat at faro.

Micah Garrick (if he is played). Tillery named him, the committee believes he is a road agent, and he was one, once, in Idaho. A party that finds out about the Boise Basin may suspect him. He had nothing to do with these robberies, and Sefton, who knows exactly who is in his gang, is pleased that the committee is looking at him.
clues: A. PATRICK KEHOE WAS INNOCENT. A1: he was on the night shift at the Number Three claim from six on the evening of 2 November to six on the morning of the 3rd, with six men, all of whom will say so if the party asks them where the committee can't hear (vg-scenario-001 or 002; Moira Kehoe names them). A2: the robbery of 3 November was at about ten in the morning, fourteen miles away, and Patrick was asleep in the boarding house from seven until noon, by Moira's word, Leonie Fairbairn's (her room is next door) and the Number Three shift boss's tally book (vg-scenario-001 or 002). A3: Konrad Kranzler's original certificate, 'death by strangulation, at the hands of persons unknown', which Grimsby tore out; the torn page is in Grimsby's wastepaper basket, or Konrad wrote a copy in his notebook (vg-scenario-001). A4: Patrick's real offence: he told the Union Saloon on 4 November that he had seen Judd Ferrier and Wick Brill leading blown horses into Fiddler's corral on the afternoon of the 3rd, when he rode up to buy hay (vg-scenario-002, from Moira or the Union's bartender, Clancy).

B. TILLERY'S CONFESSION WAS COACHED. B1: Tillery's last words to Gabriel Tennant, near dawn on 6 November: 'The man said I'd live if I gave the names he gave me. He lied, didn't he, Reverend.' (vg-scenario-001 to 003, when Gabriel trusts the party). B2: the committee's guard roster for Wexford's root cellar, in Grimsby's hand: '5 Nov, night, No. 23 (vol.)'; number 23 stood the whole night alone, at his own request (vg-scenario-002 or 003, from Wexford or Grimsby's papers). B3: half the names on the list are men Tillery barely knew: Tillery had never spoken to Barnabas Wyndham, had never been to the Beaverhead Crossing, and could not have known that Leonie Fairbairn's bank was owed money by anyone; the Union's bartender and Tillery's old bunkmate can say so (vg-scenario-002). B4: Davy Renner, if taken alive and protected: 'Warrick told Jack he'd get him out. Warrick was the one gave him the names.' (vg-scenario-003 or 004).

C. THE TWELFTH NAME CAME FROM THE MAIL. C1: the list itself: name 12 is in pencil, in a different hand, below a ruled line, and names a man nobody in camp had heard of (vg-scenario-002). C2: Barnabas Wyndham's ledger and Jack Tillery's arrest: Tillery was locked in Wexford's root cellar at three in the afternoon of Friday 4 November; the up coach carrying the marshal's letter about Hartigan was snowbound at Fiddler's Station that night and reached Ninebark at four on Saturday 5 November (vg-scenario-002). C3: Simeon Prothero kept the letter; its wafer seal is doubled, one wafer stuck over the remains of another, and he remarked on it to Barnabas at the time (vg-scenario-002). C4: Grimsby or Wexford, if turned: 'Number 23 brought us that name at the Executive on the ninth. He said Tillery told him in the cellar.' (vg-scenario-003). C5: the coach driver, Ike Leach, and the station's hostler, Jemmy: the mail sack was carried into Sefton's house for the night, 'to keep it dry', on 4 November (vg-scenario-002 or 004).

D. THE ROAD AGENTS WORK OUT OF FIDDLER'S STATION. D1: Barnabas's ledger: every robbed coach was a Thursday coach carrying more than $20,000, and the only place on the road where its weight could be learned after it left Ninebark is Fiddler's, where the boxes are moved (vg-scenario-001 or 002). D2: the tracks of 17 November go back up through the timber toward the station, not down toward the Crossing, and the horses wear Gabriel Tennant's toe-clip shoes, which he forges only for the express company's string at Fiddler's (vg-scenario-001; Survival DC 13, or Ada's Trailcraft; Gabriel recognises a cast shoe or a drawing). D3: Chelo Arvizu saw five riders lead their horses out of the timber and into Fiddler's barn on the night before the 20 October robbery (vg-scenario-002). D4: Patrick Kehoe's sighting of Ferrier and Brill with blown horses at Fiddler's corral on the afternoon of 3 November, repeated by Moira and by the Union's bartender (vg-scenario-002). D5: the washing: two shirts and a red blanket on Fiddler's line on every robbery Thursday and on no other day; visible from the coach, from the ridge, and in the memory of every driver who wondered about it once (vg-scenario-001, Perception DC 14 on the ride down; vg-scenario-002 from Benicio Aranda or Ike Leach). D6: under the barn floor at Fiddler's, a dug pit lined with planks, empty now but with gold dust in the cracks (vg-scenario-004).

E. WARRICK SEFTON IS NUMBER 23 AND THE ROAD AGENTS' CHIEF. E1: the committee's roll in Wexford's safe, numbers against names; 23 is Sefton (vg-scenario-003, from Wexford). E2: Davy Renner's or Nels Eklund's testimony, if taken alive (vg-scenario-003 or 004). E3: Moira Kehoe's account book shows Davy Renner's room was paid for in advance by Warrick Sefton, who visited him on 2 November with a basket of food 'for the poor boy who fell on a pick'; Moira thought it was kindness (vg-scenario-002). E4: in Deadfall Canyon, a letter from Sefton to Ferrier, unsigned, in the hand of the pencil name on the list: 'Last one Thursday 22nd. The Crossing road. Burn it after. Bring a man' (vg-scenario-004). E5: Sefton himself, in a showdown, or when he sees the list in a court.
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve the case when they stop asking who on the list is guilty and start asking who wrote the list. The pencil name is the hinge: nobody in Ninebark had heard of C. Hartigan, Tillery was locked up before the letter arrived, and the letter spent a night at Fiddler's Station. Point the second scenario's clues (B and C) hard, and let Cormac Hartigan's name on the list be the thing a companion cannot stop thinking about. If the party reaches vg-scenario-003 without suspecting the station, have Barnabas Wyndham, reading over his ledger by Moira's stove, say aloud: 'Every one of them. Every robbed coach changed horses at Fiddler's.'
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. THE ROAD AGENTS: Sefton falls only on evidence that a court can hear: Davy Renner's or Nels Eklund's sworn testimony, plus the doubled wafer and the pencil name, or the cache, or the letter from Deadfall Canyon. Then Judge Marten's examining court binds him over for the territorial court at Bannack in the spring, and the territorial court hangs him lawfully, or does not, which is the court's business. Ferrier, Brill and Crewe may die in the fight on the grade or in the canyon; Davy Renner, if he testifies, gets five years. If the party lets the committee have Sefton, he is hanged at the slaughter corral by the same men he used, and it is a lynching all the same: the GM narrates it as such, and the camp never learns the whole truth. THE COMMITTEE: if Wexford is turned and the Hartigan name is shown to the Executive or to a miners' meeting, the committee splits and most of it does not come out again; Pottinger and a dozen hardliners may still try on 22 December. If the party exposes the committee's roll, the Sentinel prints it, and Ninebark spends twenty years not talking about who was on it. If the party joins it, or stands by, the committee goes on hanging into the spring, as the real committees did. THE LIST: every name the party saves is a person who lives: Wyndham, Corder, Ruhl, McGarvey, Torvald Fjeld, Micah Garrick, Leonie Fairbairn, Moira Kehoe, Cormac Hartigan. Patrick Kehoe's name can be cleared in Judge Marten's court in writing, which is what Moira wants most. THE EPILOGUE: Christmas Eve, Moira Kehoe's parlour, the piano nobody can play, snow falling on the gulch. Say who is there, and whose name is not.
